title: 5 Muscles to Strengthen as You Age
summary: We all know we need to strength train to move well and feel strong. But which exercises are the most important?

As the years tick by, our body’s machinery starts to lose a little of its power. Muscles weaken, tendons tighten and movements that once felt effortless can become more difficult. The best way to[maintain strength](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/03/20/well/move/lifting-weights-exercise-older-aging-muscles-psychology.html) and mobility is through exercise,[especially weight training](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/26/well/move/greysteel-powerlifting-senior-gym.html) .


But what are the most important parts to train? With more than 600 muscles in the human body, where should you focus your attention as you age?


We put that question to physical therapy and rehabilitation experts and asked them which muscles you should prioritize as you get older.


## Butt Muscles and Quads


The most important muscles for aging are the ones that drive us through everyday movements, like getting out of bed and climbing stairs. Asked to pick one muscle group, experts said[glutes were probably the most important](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/25/well/move/strong-glutes-health-longevity.html) , because they keep your pelvis level when you walk and help recover your balance when you stumble, particularly when you need to step sideways.


“I come at this as a physical therapist and somebody who specializes in fall prevention, so that’s what I’m thinking about,” said Odessa Addison, a professor of physical therapy and rehabilitation science at the University of Maryland School of Medicine.


Most people who exercise regularly are familiar with the largest of the gluteal muscles, the gluteus maximus, and target it with classic movements like[squats](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/04/26/well/move/squat-technique.html) and[dead lifts](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/02/14/well/move/romanian-deadlift-technique.html) .
